introduction_markdown: Multiple choice paper (0560 History 1, June 2021, Ordinary Level, Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board). One and a half hours. Answer ALL the 50 questions in this Examination; all questions carry equal marks. Non-programmable calculators are allowed. Each question has FOUR suggested answers A, B, C and D: mark only one answer for each question (more than one answer scores zero for that question). The paper has three parts, all compulsory: Section A, Cameroon since 1850 (questions 1-25); Section B, Africa since 1870 (excluding Cameroon) (questions 26-40); Section C, World Diplomacy since 1870 (questions 41-50).
enonce_intro_markdown: **Multiple choice questions** - choose the one correct answer, A, B, C or D. Section A: Cameroon since 1850 (questions 1-25). Section B: Africa since 1870 (excluding Cameroon) (questions 26-40). Section C: World Diplomacy since 1870 (questions 41-50).
incertitudes: Converties en questions ouvertes par le relecteur (clé ou options discutables) : 3, 20, 25.

Page de garde verifiee : 0560 HISTORY 1, JUNE 2021, ORDINARY LEVEL, Multiple Choice Question Paper, One and a half hours, Answer ALL the 50 questions, calculatrices non programmables permises. Sections imprimees : A Cameroon since 1850 (Q1-25), B Africa since 1870 excluding Cameroon (Q26-40), C World Diplomacy since 1870 (Q41-50). Aucune regle de choix : regles_choix et groupes vides. 6 pages lues en image (rendu sans calques de filigrane, regime A_calques) ; le texte de verso qui transparait et les filigranes ont ete ignores ; aucune figure dans ce sujet.

Aucun corrige officiel : les cles sont deduites du programme d'histoire du GCE (Cameroun, Afrique, monde depuis 1870) et par elimination. Faits a faible marge d'incertitude, a relire par un historien avant mise en avant : Q4 (les agents de Woermann, Schmidt et Voss, ont signe le traite de juillet 1884 ; le role exact de la maison est presente de facon un peu differente selon les manuels) ; Q5 (Rogozinski et Janikowski etaient des explorateurs polonais ; la formule du sujet 'on behalf of Britain' est reprise telle quelle, elle n'est pas verifiee) ; Q6 (liste exacte des ecoles d'agriculture allemandes : Victoria, Yaounde et Dschang donnees par prudence, Douala retenu comme intrus) ; Q7 (Bangwa retenu par elimination : Bakweri 1891, Fulbe vers 1899-1901, Douala jusqu'en 1914 ; la date de la resistance bangwa est approximative, 'mid-1900s') ; Q12 (1922 = confirmation des mandats par la SDN ; 1919 partage provisoire, 1920 entree en vigueur du traite de Versailles) ; Q13 (Chief Manga Williams comme representant des Cameroons sous la constitution Clifford : attribution des manuels, date non precisee dans le corrige) ; Q17 (Endeley, premier titulaire du titre de Premier en 1958, remplace par Foncha en 1959) ; Q35 (l'independance de la Libye en 1951 existe, mais la reponse classique est la croissance du nationalisme) ; Q41 (l'Allemagne s'industrialisait rapidement en 1870 : le Portugal reste le seul pays non industrialise).

Q3, Q20 et Q25 : questions passees en OUVERTES par le relecteur (cle ou options defectueuses). Q3 : aucune option n'est un resultat immediat exact de l'Acte de Berlin pour le Cameroun (le traite germano-duala de 1884 n'a pas ete abandonne, la traite etait finie, le commerce legitime etait ancien) ; reponse visee formulee dans le corrige (regle de l'occupation effective), sans lettre. Q20 : la West Cameroon Development Agency (organisme economique) est retenue comme exception visee, mais la Federal House of Assembly (institution federale) peut aussi etre defendue ; lettre B indiquee comme reponse visee. Q25 : l'organisation rejointe en 1995 est le Commonwealth, absent des options imprimees (UDFAC [sic], Francophonie, CEMAC, A.U) ; aucune lettre.

Fautes d'impression laissees telles quelles dans les enonces : 'UDFAC' (UDEAC) Q25, 'Philipe Leclerc' Q18, 'Kofi Busa' (Busia) Q39, 'Fritz Nansen' (Fridtjof) Q48, 'Haile Selassie II' (Ier) Q34, 'King Mohammed II of Morocco' Q34, 'Jesco' (Jesko) Q7 ; signalees dans le corrige quand elles comptent. Une marque d'encre isolee pres de l'option C de la Q16 et des taches en marge ont ete ignorees.
Aucun calcul numerique dans ce sujet (histoire) : rien a recalculer avec Python.

Seconde passe faite : les 6 pages du PDF ont ete relues en image et les 50 questions resolues une deuxieme fois independamment ; enonces et options conformes au sujet (fautes d'impression conservees), aucune cle modifiee a l'issue de la seconde passe.

questions.enonce_markdown: By what name was the institution set up in Douala by the British consular officials to regulate trade in 1856 called?
questions.corrige_markdown: In 1856 the Duala chiefs, the European (mostly British) traders on the river and the British consular officials created in Douala a body to settle trade disputes, enforce the payment of debts (the trade was run on credit, or "trust") and keep order in the trade. It was known as the **Court of Equity**. The other names are not the name of this Douala body: a Consular Court is a court held by a consul for his own nationals, and a Court of Justice or a Merchant Maritime Court is not what the Duala trade institution was called. **Answer: C.**
themes: european trade on the cameroon coast

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following coastal towns was firmly under British control on the eve of the annexation of Cameroon?
questions.corrige_markdown: Victoria (today Limbe) was founded in 1858 by the English Baptist missionary Alfred Saker and his followers, and it remained a British-oriented settlement closely tied to the British Baptist Mission and to British consular influence. Campo, Grand Batanga and Malimba were not under firm British control: they were small coastal trading places where German and other firms were active. The answer is therefore Victoria. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The **immediate** result of the signing of the Berlin Act of 1885 on the scramble and partition of Cameroon was...

*Options as printed:* A) the abandonment of the Germano-Duala Treaty of 1884   B) the stoppage of the slave trade in the 1880s   C) the introduction of legitimate trade   D) the spread of Christianity in the interior of Cameroon
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Berlin Conference (November 1884 to February 1885) ended with the Berlin Act of 26 February 1885. It set rules for the scramble: freedom of trade and navigation on the Congo and Niger, a condemnation of the slave trade, protection for missionaries, and the rule that a power claiming new coast had to notify the others and occupy it effectively. For Cameroon, the Germano-Duala Treaty of July 1884 came before the Act and was not abandoned: it remained the basis of the German claim (so option A is false). The slave trade on this coast had ended long before the 1880s (B is weak), legitimate trade had begun early in the 19th century (C is false), and the spread of Christianity in the interior was a slow later development linked only indirectly to the Act (D). No printed option is a clean, accurate immediate result.

**Expected answer: the Act's rule of effective occupation pushed Germany to consolidate its Cameroon claim (no printed option fits cleanly).**



The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: An **important** contribution of the Carl Woermann Firm in the colonisation of Cameroon was...
questions.corrige_markdown: The Hamburg firm of Woermann (led by Adolph Woermann) pressed Bismarck to take a protectorate over the Cameroon coast to protect German trade. In July 1884 its agents (Edward Schmidt and Johannes Voss, together with the agent of the firm Jantzen and Thormaehlen) concluded the Germano-Duala Treaty with the Duala kings Bell and Akwa, and Gustav Nachtigal proclaimed the German protectorate. The firm did not sponsor British annexation and did not hold meetings with French traders. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: it held annexation meetings with the French traders
it was very harsh on anti-German propaganda

questions.enonce_markdown: The **two** Polish agents who signed **treaties** on behalf of Britain with Bakweri chiefs from Bota to Rio Del Rey during the scramble for the Cameroon coast were...
questions.corrige_markdown: The two Poles of the scramble on the Cameroon coast were the explorers Stefan Szolc-Rogozinski and Leopold Janikowski, who were in the Bimbia and Mount Cameroon area in the early 1880s and made agreements with local (Bakweri and neighbouring) chiefs. Edward Hewett was the British consul, who arrived in 1884 just after the Germans, and Edward Schmidt and Johannes Voss were the German agents of the Woermann firm. So the pair asked for is Rogozinski and Janikowski. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: In order to promote agricultural development in German Kamerun, the German colonial Governor established agricultural schools in the following places **except**...
questions.corrige_markdown: To train Africans in modern farming and to support the plantations, the German administration set up agricultural training schools and stations at places such as Victoria (near the botanical garden), Yaounde and Dschang in the highlands. Douala was mainly the port, trading and administrative centre of the colony, and it is the odd one out in the list. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which was the last and final native resistance to German rule that Governor Jesco Von Puttkamer crushed by 1906?
questions.corrige_markdown: Governor Jesko von Puttkamer ruled from 1895 to 1907. Among the four resistances, the Bakweri resistance around Buea was crushed in the early 1890s, the Fulbe resistance in Adamawa was broken at the turn of the century (about 1899-1901), and the Douala resistance lasted until Rudolf Duala Manga Bell was executed in 1914, long after Puttkamer had left office. That leaves the Bangwa resistance of the mid-1900s as the last one he put down. **Answer: C.**
themes: indigenous resistance to german rule in cameroon

questions.enonce_markdown: Question 8 is based on these remarks about a German Governor in Cameroon "... he initiated gigantic public works, established plantations, created Gesellschaft Sud Kamerun and Gesellschaft Nord West Kamerun to promote German trade on the territory...yet his rule was marked by scandals ..." Who was the German Governor referred to above?
questions.corrige_markdown: The concession companies Gesellschaft Sued-Kamerun and Gesellschaft Nordwest-Kamerun were created in 1899 under Governor Jesko von Puttkamer (governor from 1895 to 1907). His rule saw many public works and the growth of the plantations, but also forced labour, harsh punishments and scandals that led to his recall in 1907. Von Soden was the first governor (1885-1891), Von Zimmerer ruled in 1891-1895 and Seitz in 1907-1910. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The Cameroonian traditional ruler whose collaboration with the Germans facilitated German expansion in the Western Grass Fields was...
questions.corrige_markdown: Fon Galega I of Bali-Nyonga allied with the Germans (first with Eugen Zintgraff, then with the later German officers) and supplied warriors and carriers, which helped them to extend their control over the Grassfields against neighbours such as the Bafut. The other names do not match this role. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following battles gave the Allies a strategic naval base for World War I in Cameroon?
questions.corrige_markdown: The Anglo-French forces captured Douala in September 1914. Douala was the main port, with its harbour and wireless station, so its fall gave the Allies a naval base on the coast. Nsanakang (September 1914) was a German success near the Nigerian border, Garoua in the north fell in 1915, and Yaounde was taken only in January 1916. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The partition of Cameroon between the British and the French led to the division of the following ethnic groups with the **exception** of....
questions.corrige_markdown: The Anglo-French frontier of 1919 cut across several peoples of the western highlands and the forest belt, such as the Bakossi and the Mbo (between the British Kumba area and the French Nkongsamba area) and the Bamileke groups living along the border. The Ewondo live around Yaounde, deep inside the French zone, so they were not divided. **Answer: D.**
themes: partition of cameroon after world war one

questions.enonce_markdown: Which date marked the start of the British Mandate in Cameroon?
questions.corrige_markdown: The Milner-Simon Declaration of July 1919 provisionally shared Cameroon between Britain and France, and the Treaty of Versailles came into force in January 1920. The League of Nations, however, confirmed the British and French Class B Mandates over their parts of Cameroon in July 1922, and this is the date generally given for the start of the British Mandate. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify the Southern Cameroons traditional ruler who represented the territory in the Legislative Council in Nigeria under the Clifford Constitution.
questions.corrige_markdown: Chief John Manga Williams of Victoria is the traditional ruler remembered as the Cameroons representative in the Nigerian Legislative Council under the Clifford Constitution of 1922. Fon Galega II (Bali) and Fon Achirimbi II (Bafut) were Grassfields rulers, and E.M.L. Endeley was a politician and doctor who came to the front only from the 1940s. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify the French economic policy in Cameroon during the Mandate period which was aimed at exploiting the economic resources of the territory for the benefit of France.
questions.corrige_markdown: La mise en valeur ("development" of the colonies, associated with the Sarraut plan of 1921) was the French economic policy of making the colony's resources (cocoa, coffee, timber, palm products, rubber, railways and roads) serve the French economy. Prestation (labour tax) and corvee (forced labour) were methods used to carry it out, and assimilation was a cultural and administrative policy. **Answer: D.**
themes: french rule in cameroon under the mandate

questions.enonce_markdown: The Second World War had all the following effects on Cameroonians **except**...
questions.corrige_markdown: The partition of Cameroon between Britain and France was a result of the First World War (1919), not of the Second. The Second World War brought hardship to Cameroonians: forced labour and requisitions, high taxes, shortages, unemployment and disruption of schooling, as well as a rise in political awareness. **Answer: A.**
themes: impact of world war two on africa

questions.enonce_markdown: Under which Southern Cameroons nationalist leader did the people of the region gain a Quasi-Federal status in 1954?
questions.corrige_markdown: In 1954 the Lyttelton Constitution gave Southern Cameroons a quasi-federal status in the Federation of Nigeria, with its own House of Assembly in Buea. The leader of the government at that time was Dr. E.M.L. Endeley of the Kamerun National Congress. Foncha came to power only in 1959. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify the **political** personality who in May 1958 became Southern Cameroons first Premier.
questions.corrige_markdown: After Southern Cameroons became a self-governing region, its leader Dr. E.M.L. Endeley took the title of Premier in 1958, the first holder of this title, until J.N. Foncha replaced him in 1959 after the elections. Muna and Foncha were later figures, and Eyo Ita was a Nigerian (Eastern Region) politician. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The French High Commissioner often associated with the banning of the U.P.C in French Cameroon in the 1950s was...
questions.corrige_markdown: The UPC was banned in July 1955 under the High Commissioner Roland Pre, after the troubles of May 1955. Richard Brunot was an earlier High Commissioner, Pierre Messmer (1956-1958) came after Pre, and Philippe Leclerc was the Free French general of the Second World War. **Answer: B.**
themes: upc and french repression in cameroon

questions.enonce_markdown: For what reason was 1st June 1961 declared a day of national mourning for Cameroon by Ahidjo?
questions.corrige_markdown: In the plebiscite of February 1961 Northern Cameroons voted to join Nigeria, and on 1 June 1961 it became part of Nigeria. President Ahidjo, who had hoped to see the whole of British Cameroons join the Republic of Cameroon, declared 1 June 1961 a day of national mourning for this loss. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: Loss of British Northern Cameroons to Nigeria
The atrocities of the UPC party in Southern Cameroons
Southern Cameroons voted to re-join the Republic of Cameroon
The torture of Southern Cameroonians by Nigerians

questions.enonce_markdown:
The following were important **social and political** structures in the Federated state of West Cameroon in the 1960s **except**...

*Options as printed:* A) West Cameroon House of Assembly   B) West Cameroon Development Agency   C) Federal House of Assembly   D) West Cameroon House of Chiefs
questions.corrige_markdown:
The West Cameroon House of Assembly and the West Cameroon House of Chiefs were institutions of the Federated State of West Cameroon. The West Cameroon Development Agency (WCDA) was an economic body (it ran plantations and development projects), not a social or political structure, and the Federal House of Assembly was a federal institution for the whole country, sitting in Yaounde. Two of the options can therefore be argued as the exception.

**Intended answer: B (West Cameroon Development Agency).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The political party in Southern Cameroons that actively supported the concept of reunification in the 1950s and 1960s was...
questions.corrige_markdown: The Kamerun National Democratic Party (KNDP) of J.N. Foncha, founded in 1955, campaigned for reunification with French Cameroun and won the 1959 elections. The CPNC (Endeley) favoured integration with Nigeria. The UPC was banned in Southern Cameroons in 1957 and was not the party that carried the reunification campaign there. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: He masterminded the abolition of the Cameroon Federation in May 1972 through a nation-wide Referendum. Identify the leader who is associated with the above description.
questions.corrige_markdown: President Ahmadou Ahidjo organised the referendum of 20 May 1972 that replaced the Federal Republic by the United Republic of Cameroon. Mbida was Prime Minister of French Cameroun in 1957-1958, Biya succeeded Ahidjo in 1982, and Foncha was Prime Minister of West Cameroon and Vice-President of the Federation. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which major educational reform did the Biya administration introduce in 1993 to reduce Anglophone agitation?
questions.corrige_markdown: In 1993, as a response to Anglophone demands for the protection of the Anglo-Saxon educational heritage, the government created the Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board (GCE Board). The Higher Teachers Training College at Bambili and the Kumba technical college came from the 1980s, and the Anglo-Saxon style university created in 1993 was at Buea, not Bamenda, so option C is wrong. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: The establishment of a Higher Technical Training College in Kumba
The opening of Higher Teachers Training College in Bambili
The creation of Anglo-Saxon University in Bamenda
The creation of the Cameroon GCE Board

questions.enonce_markdown: The first Anglophone Prime Minister under the Biya administration was...
questions.corrige_markdown: Simon Achidi Achu was appointed Prime Minister in April 1992, the first Anglophone to hold the post under President Biya. Peter Mafany Musonge succeeded him in 1996 and Philemon Yang became Prime Minister in 2009. S.T. Muna was a Vice-President and National Assembly President, not a Prime Minister. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which one of the following international organisations did Cameroon join in 1995?

*Options as printed:* A) UDFAC   B) Francophonie   C) CEMAC   D) A.U
questions.corrige_markdown:
In November 1995 Cameroon was admitted to the **Commonwealth of Nations**, together with Mozambique, which was not British: this was linked to the Anglophone question, as the Anglophone community wanted Cameroon's Anglo-Saxon heritage recognised. The Commonwealth is not among the printed options. UDEAC (written UDFAC in the paper) was created in the 1960s, the CEMAC treaty dates from 1994 and came into effect later, the African Union was launched in 2002, and Cameroon's links with the Francophone family are far older than 1995. The question as printed has no correct option.

**Expected answer: the Commonwealth of Nations (not among the options).**



The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following African river basins was the scene of colonial rivalry between Portugal and France in 1879 almost leading to war?
questions.corrige_markdown: The Congo Basin was the main focus of colonial rivalry at the start of the scramble: King Leopold II's agent Stanley, the Frenchman De Brazza and the Portuguese all claimed the mouth and banks of the Congo from about 1879. This rivalry was the direct cause of the Berlin Conference of 1884-1885. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which **economic** principle was responsible for the scramble for Africa in the 1880s?
questions.corrige_markdown: The economic cause of the scramble was capitalism: the industrialised countries of Europe needed raw materials, new markets for their goods and places to invest surplus capital. Balance of power and national prestige were political causes and white racism was an ideological cause. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The Maji Maji Rebellion in East Africa between 1905 and 1906 was staged against the colonial ambitions of...
questions.corrige_markdown: The Maji Maji rising broke out in 1905 in German East Africa (Tanganyika) against German rule, forced cotton growing and forced labour, under the religious leader Kinjikitile Ngwale who gave his followers "maji" (water) believed to protect them from bullets. The Germans crushed it, with a very heavy loss of life. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: In which of the following African territories was the Belgian policy of Paternalism practised by 1914?
questions.corrige_markdown: Paternalism treated Africans as children to be looked after (basic health and mission education) while denying them political rights. It was the Belgian policy in the Belgian Congo, which Belgium took over from Leopold II in 1908. Tanganyika was German (later British), Eritrea was Italian, and Rwanda-Urundi passed to Belgium only after 1916, so it was not Belgian in 1914. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: What did the following European colonies in Africa have in common: **Rhodesia, Angola, Kenya, and South West Africa**?
questions.corrige_markdown: Rhodesia, Angola, Kenya and South West Africa were settler colonies: they had a healthy climate and good land, so European settlers established permanent farms and homes there, often taking the best land from Africans. Indirect rule was used mainly by the British in West Africa and was not the common feature of these four. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: They were governed through Indirect Rule.
Native populations were not allowed to own land
They were backward and were not allowed to stay on their own
Whites were allowed to establish permanent homes

questions.enonce_markdown: The colonial rule that made use of **Warrant Chiefs** in areas where traditional institutions were not firmly established was called...
questions.corrige_markdown: Warrant chiefs were men given a "warrant" (an official document) by the British to rule in societies without chiefs, such as the Igbo of south-eastern Nigeria. This was a feature of British Indirect Rule, the system of governing through African rulers. Assimilation was the French policy, Association a later French idea, and Paternalism a Belgian policy. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The following African countries served as battleground for the Allies and the German forces during the First World War **except**...
questions.corrige_markdown: Fighting between the Allies and Germany took place in the German colonies: Togoland (August 1914), Kamerun, German South West Africa (1914-1915) and German East Africa, later Tanganyika (until 1918). Ethiopia was an independent country and was not a battleground in that war. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following African territories was placed under the Mandate System of the League of Nations after the First World War?
questions.corrige_markdown: Tanganyika, the former German East Africa, became a British Mandate under the League of Nations. Kenya, Southern Rhodesia and Nyasaland were British colonies, protectorates or self-governing colonies and were not taken from Germany or Turkey. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The African leader whose nation was a member of the League of Nations and was conquered in the 1930s but regained his throne in the course of World War II was...
questions.corrige_markdown: Ethiopia, a League of Nations member since 1923, was invaded by fascist Italy in 1935 and conquered in 1936. Emperor Haile Selassie appealed to the League in vain and went into exile, then regained his throne in 1941 with British help during World War II. Menelik II had died in 1913, and Egypt and Morocco were not conquered by a European power in this way in the 1930s. The printed name "Haile Selassie II" is a misprint for Haile Selassie I; the answer is not affected. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: Emperor Haile Selassie II of Ethiopia

questions.enonce_markdown: The immediate blessing of the Second World War on Africa between 1945 and 1955 was....
questions.corrige_markdown: The war weakened Britain and France, taught African ex-servicemen new ideas and raised hopes of freedom, so African nationalism grew strongly in the years that followed. Independence came for most countries only from 1957 onward, the OAU was formed in 1963, and neo-colonialism was a later development. **Answer: C.**
themes: impact of world war two on africa

questions.enonce_markdown: An **important** internal factor that promoted African nationalism after 1945 was...
questions.corrige_markdown: An internal factor comes from inside Africa. After 1945, trade unions, pressure groups and political parties spread and mobilised the people against colonial rule. The creation of the UNO in 1945 was an external factor, colonial powers did not promise independence at that time, and the West African Students' Union was formed in London in 1925, long before 1945. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: rise of pressure groups and political parties
promise of independence to Africa by colonial masters
formation of West African Students' Union

questions.enonce_markdown: Which group of Africans as a result of the Second World War mounted pressure on the colonial powers for the decolonisation of their territories?
questions.corrige_markdown: The western-educated elites (teachers, clerks, lawyers, journalists, trade unionists) led the demands for self-rule and independence, as they understood the principles of the Atlantic Charter and the United Nations and the weakness of the colonial powers after the war. Missionaries were Europeans, and market women and farmers did not lead the political campaign. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify the Biafran leader whose political activities contributed to the outbreak of a bloody civil war in his country in the 1960s.
questions.corrige_markdown: Colonel Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu, military governor of Eastern Nigeria, declared the Republic of Biafra in May 1967, which led to the Nigerian civil war (1967-1970). Effiong was his deputy who signed the surrender in 1970, Ironsi was Nigeria's first military ruler in 1966, and Gowon was the federal leader on the other side. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The following Ghanaian Heads of State headed military regimes. Identify the one who headed both military and civilian regimes.
questions.corrige_markdown: Jerry John Rawlings led the military coup of 1979 and ruled again as head of the military PNDC from 1981, then was elected president in 1992 and 1996 and ruled a civilian, constitutional government until 2001. Ankrah and Acheampong were purely military heads of state, and Kofi Busia (the printed "Busa") was a civilian prime minister overthrown by the army in 1972. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The Pan African organisation that replaced the O.A.U by 2002 was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: The Organisation of African Unity (founded in 1963) was replaced in 2002 by the African Union, launched in Durban. The "United States of Africa" was Nkrumah's idea and the other names are not real successors. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following European countries had **not** acquired an industrialised economy by 1870?
questions.corrige_markdown: By 1870 Britain was the first industrial power, France was industrialised and Germany was industrialising fast and soon overtook Britain in steel and chemicals. Portugal remained a mainly agricultural country with little industry. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The Bismarckian Alliance System of isolating France suffered a setback in 1892 with the formation of...
questions.corrige_markdown: Bismarck's system aimed to keep France without allies. It broke down when Germany let the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia lapse in 1890 and Russia moved towards France: the Franco-Russian alliance was agreed in 1892 (military convention) and confirmed in 1894. The Austro-German Dual Alliance (1879) and the Triple Alliance (1882) were part of Bismarck's own system, and the Triple Entente came in 1907. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify the particular new type of battleship whose contribution in the 1900s sparked-off the naval race between Germany and Britain that contributed to the outbreak of the First World War.
questions.corrige_markdown: The British launched HMS Dreadnought in 1906, a heavily armed and fast battleship that made older ships out of date. Germany answered with its own dreadnoughts under Admiral Tirpitz, and the Anglo-German naval race that followed increased tension before 1914. U-boats were important in the war itself and aircraft carriers came later. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: In which city did the assassination of Franz Ferdinand take place on 28th June 1914 leading to the outbreak of the First World War?
questions.corrige_markdown: Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, was shot in Sarajevo (Bosnia) on 28 June 1914 by the Serb nationalist Gavrilo Princip. This was the immediate cause of the war. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The European power, who prior to the outbreak of the First World War was at the centre of European diplomacy but suffered defeat during the war and humiliation at the Paris Peace Settlement was...
questions.corrige_markdown: Germany had been at the centre of European diplomacy since Bismarck and was defeated in 1918. At Paris it was blamed for the war (war guilt clause), disarmed, lost territory and colonies and had to pay reparations under the Treaty of Versailles. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The international agreement which paved the way for the admission of Germany into the League of Nations in the 1920s was...
questions.corrige_markdown: In the Locarno Treaties of 1925 Germany accepted its western frontiers with France and Belgium, and Germany was admitted to the League of Nations in 1926. The Treaty of Rapallo (1922) was a German-Soviet agreement, the Dawes Plan (1924) dealt with reparations, and the Briand-Kellogg Pact (1928) condemned war. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The **two** Japanese cities that were devastated by the dropping of atomic bombs in August 1945, bringing the Second World War to an end were...
questions.corrige_markdown: The United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima (6 August 1945) and Nagasaki (9 August 1945), and Japan surrendered soon after. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The European diplomat who served as the **first** Secretary General of the League of Nations at its creation in 1919 was...
questions.corrige_markdown: Sir Eric Drummond, a British diplomat, was the first Secretary General of the League of Nations (1920-1933). Smuts was a South African statesman who helped to draft the idea of the League, Albert Thomas was the first director of the International Labour Organisation, and Fridtjof Nansen was the League's High Commissioner for Refugees. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which agency of the United Nations Organisation is concerned mainly with war against illiteracy and cultural decadence?
questions.corrige_markdown: UNESCO, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation, deals with education (including the fight against illiteracy), science and culture. FAO deals with food and agriculture, UNICEF with children and WHO with health. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A refugee is all of the following **except**...
questions.corrige_markdown: A refugee is a person forced to flee his or her country by war, persecution or a disaster and who seeks safety elsewhere. A migrant worker who moves freely to find better opportunities is moving by choice, not forced by danger, so this is not a refugee. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: One who flees his country because of a natural disaster
Migrant worker seeking for better opportunities in another country
One who finds refuge in another country because of political persecution
One who flees his country because of war
